citation.title: Changing Climates of Conflict: A Social Network Experiment in 56 Schools

standing_assumptions:
The article (PNAS 113(3):566–571; printed pp. 566–571 are main PDF pp. 1–6) and its SI Appendix (43 pages; the printed page number equals the supplement PDF page number) state no theorem, proposition or lemma and give no proof. Their formal objects are the school-level regressions (SI Eqs. (1)–(6)), the exposure mapping, the exposure probabilities and the inverse-probability-weighted regression estimator (SI pp. 16–19), one sentence of asymptotic justification (SI p. 19) and the notes to Tables S6 and S7. There are two official corrections: PNAS 115(15):E3598 (2018), which replaces 30% by 25%, and a 2019 correction that adds a grant number. Everything quoted below was read from the rendered page images.
(S1) Schools and blocks. SI p. 5 (Study design): “Prior to randomization, schools agreed to participate in all measurement aspects of the program, with a 50% chance of receiving the anti-conflict program (the treatment).” “Schools were assigned to blocks of four, and randomized to receive the treatment or not within these blocks.” “Four schools dropped out from the study before the point of randomization, which left the total sample at 56 schools and 24,191 students.” Fig. S1, caption (SI p. 24): “The 56 schools were first blocked into groups of four by pretreatment school level variables including size and student demographics (see SI). Within each of the 14 school blocks, two schools were assigned to control (the two school networks on the left), and two to treatment, the anti-conflict intervention (the two school networks on the right). The nodes depict the population of students at the school. Grey nodes are the “seed eligible” students, selected by a deterministic algorithm and comprising a representative sample of the school. Seed eligibles were blocked into four equally sized groups based on pretreatment characteristics including gender and grade, and half of the students in each block were randomly assigned to be treated (part of the anti-conflict program) if they were in a treatment school; dark green nodes are treated seed eligibles. Nodes in the shape of stars are the social referents, who are in the top 10% of their school in connections reported by other students in the pre-randomization survey.”
(S2) Seed-eligibles and seeds. SI p. 6, with $a_i$ a student's indegree and $b_i$ the student's closure: “The students in each of the gender-grade-$b_i$ blocks with the largest values of $a_i$ were considered eligible for randomization into the seed group, such that we had no fewer than 40 seed-eligible students (schools with fewer than 200 students), and no more than 64 seed-eligible students (schools with less than 550 students). For schools with between 200 and 550, we scaled linearly between 40 and 64 seed-eligible students, rounding to the nearest 4. Table S2 demonstrates the covariate profiles of eligible and ineligible students. All of our estimates are computed conditional on the composition of the seed-eligible groups. Among treated schools, half of the seed-eligibles were block-randomized into the seed group, using 4 blocks constructed using gender, grade, and $b_i$ (using an R package, blockTools).” Main p. 567 (PDF p. 2): “In the 28 of 56 schools randomly assigned to receive the intervention, we selected a group of students (the seed-eligibles) using a deterministic algorithm (see SI Appendix for materials and methods used) designed to represent 15% of the school population, blocked by gender and grade and capped at 64 students (grades ranged from 5 to 8) (SI Appendix, Figs. S1 and S2, and Table S1). We randomly assigned 50% of that group (the seeds) to be invited to participate in the anticonflict intervention, which our team implemented over the course of the school year. Within each seed group at each school (on average 26 seeds at each school, for a total of 728 seeds across 28 schools), a random proportion were social referent seeds, meaning they were in the top 10% of their school in the number of connections reported by other students (i.e., indegree).”
(S3) School-level (climate) regressions. SI p. 13: “We fit the following linear regression model: $Y_{ij} = \alpha_j + \tau D_{ij} + \gamma C^E_{ij} + u_{ij}$ (1) where $ij$ denotes the $i$th school in the $j$th block. $Y_{ij}$ denotes school-level outcomes, $\alpha_j$ is a block-level fixed effect, $D_{ij}$ is the school-level treatment assignment, $C_{ij}$ is the composition of the seed group (percentage of seed group that is classified as a social referent), and $C^E_{ij}$ is the composition of the seed eligible group (percentage of seed eligible group that is classified as a social referent). $\tau$ here is the average causal effect of treatment. We include $C^E_{ij}$ as a covariate control here so as to maximize comparability with the interaction model in (4). In all cases, the model is fit with OLS regression with heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors to characterize uncertainty.” The interaction model, Eq. (2) (repeated as Eq. (4)), and its interpretation are transcribed in P037-T14. SI p. 16: “This amounts to fitting the following model for main effects: $Y_{ij} = \alpha_j + \tau D_{ij} + \gamma C^E_{ij} + \boldsymbol{\theta}\mathbf{X}_{ij} + u_{ij}$, (5) where $\mathbf{X}_{ij}$ is a vector of school-specific pretreatment covariates (percentage white, percentage English-speaking, average house quality and, where available, pretreatment measurement of $Y_{ij}$).” Main p. 568 (PDF p. 3): “We computed confidence intervals and P values using robust SEs under a normal approximation.” Main p. 567: “(Administrative data were available for 49 of the 56 schools, and we restricted our attention to these schools for analyses of conflict-related events.)”
(S4) Scale of composition. In the targets $C_{ij}$ and $C^E_{ij}$ are fractions in $[0,1]$ (0.20 means 20%), the scale of Fig. 2 and Table S7. The SI's wording (“percentage”, “$c\%$”, “percentage points”) does not match that scale; this is finding P037-N020, rated a clarity note, and is not a target.
(S5) Social-influence setting. SI pp. 16–17: “We have a finite population of students indexed by $i = 1, ..., N$ on which our randomized experiment is performed. Define a treatment assignment vector, $\mathbf{z} = (z_1, ..., z_N)'$, where $z_i \in \{0, 1\}$ denotes whether or not student $i$ is assigned to be a seed (i.e., is invited to participate in the anti-conflict group). An experimental design is a plan for randomly selecting a particular value of $\mathbf{z}$ with predetermined probability $p_{\mathbf{z}}$. Restricting our attention only to treatment assignments that can be generated by our experimental design, define $\Omega = \{\mathbf{z} : p_{\mathbf{z}} > 0\}$, so that $\mathbf{Z} = (Z_1, ..., Z_N)'$ is a random vector with support $\Omega$ and $\Pr(\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{z}) = p_{\mathbf{z}}$. In this setting, treatment assignment is the random assignment of seeds both across and within schools according our hierarchical randomization (i.e., so that half of schools are assigned to control schools with no seeds).” The exposure mapping $f(\mathbf{z},\theta_i)$ with $\theta_i$, $\gamma$ and $s_i$ (SI p. 17) is transcribed in P037-T7. SI p. 18: “We allow for each student $i$ to have a vector of potential outcomes, which we denote by $(y_i(d_C), ...y_i(d_D))$, that do not depend on the value of $\mathbf{Z}$. We seek estimates for $k \in \{C, S, NI, I\}$ (i.e., control exposure, school exposure, non-social referent peer exposure, social referent peer exposure) of the average potential outcome $\mu(d_k) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} y_i(d_k)$.” “$\pi_i(d_k) = \sum_{\mathbf{z}\in\Omega} \mathbf{I}(f(\mathbf{z},\theta_i) = d_k)\Pr(\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{z})$.” “We restrict ourselves to the subpopulation of students (n=2451) for which there exists some probability that students could receive all four exposures: $0 < \pi_i(d_k) < 1$ for $k \in \{C, S, NI, I\}$.” The estimator $\widehat{\mu_R}(d_k)$ (SI p. 19) is transcribed in P037-T11.
(S6) None of the eleven headline claims (P037-H1 to P037-H11) is a mathematical statement: each is an empirical estimate, a description of the design or an interpretive conclusion. Every target below therefore comes from a confirmed error.
(S7) [Added on 6 October 2026, after the authors' analysis code became available; it applies to the revised P037-T2 and to P037-T18 onward.] The authors' eleven R scripts, as released by ICPSR with study 37070, were not available when (S1)–(S6) and P037-T1 to T17 were written. In the targets added or revised afterwards, ‘the released code’ means those scripts as read and run by the checkers; a statement of what the code does is established by the code and is not a statement of the publication. ‘On the public data’ means a value obtained from the public data release (ICPSR 37070 V2) run through the authors' scripts with an adapter, or from a reconstruction on that release; the authors' own analysis files are not public and ICPSR states that some variables in the release were changed, so such a value is not the value the authors would obtain from their own files. No such value is part of a target's statement: the statements are exact identities, probabilities, counts and counterexamples, and values on the public data appear only in notes, as aggregates (the data are respondent-level records of school students; no respondent row and no school identifier is given). The scripts are cited by number: script 1, ‘1. Sanitize and generate perms, probs.R’ (the network, referent status, the simulated seed and school assignments, the exposure indicators and their simulated probabilities); script 2, ‘2. Cleaning.R’ (outcomes and covariates); script 3, ‘3. Network results.R’ (the social-influence estimates and their randomization standard errors); script 4, ‘4. School results-with-correction.R’ (the school-level regressions, their three kinds of standard error, the percentages of the 2018 Correction and Fig. 2); script 6, ‘6. Bond et al analysis.R’ (Fig. S5). Line numbers are those of the released files, as cited by the checkers.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Main Methods, ‘We computed confidence intervals and P values using robust SEs under a normal approximation’; the heteroskedasticity-robust Wald tests of Results (first paragraph) and of the Fig. 2 caption; SI p. 13 and the rows ‘Heteroskedasticity Robust SE’ and ‘Wild Bootstrap SE’ of Tables S6 and S7 for peer conflict, as printed
canonical_claim.location: main p. 568 (PDF p. 3); main p. 569 (PDF p. 4), Results and Fig. 2 caption; SI p. 13 (supplement PDF p. 13); SI Tables S6 and S7, pp. 41–42 (supplement PDF pp. 41–42)
canonical_claim.statement:
[Main p. 568, Methods] “We computed confidence intervals and P values using robust SEs under a normal approximation.”
[Main p. 569, Results] “Figs. 1 and 2 reveal that the treatment significantly reduced average levels of disciplinary reports of peer conflict in treatment compared with control schools ($P < 0.05$, heteroskedasticity-robust Wald test).”
[Main p. 569, Fig. 2 caption] “We find that a higher proportion of social referent seeds assigned to the anticonflict group increases the size of the overall school effect on disciplinary reports of peer conflict ($P$ = 0.07, heteroskedasticity-robust Wald test).”
[SI p. 13] “In all cases, the model is fit with OLS regression with heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors to characterize uncertainty.”
[Table S6, SI p. 41, column Peer conflict] School level main effect: $-0.06$; Heteroskedasticity Robust SE: $(0.03)$; Wild Bootstrap SE: $(0.03)$. [Table S7, SI p. 42, column Peer conflict] Interaction: Proportion of Referents in Treatment group: $-0.85$; Heteroskedasticity Robust SE: $(0.46)$; Wild Bootstrap SE: $(0.47)$. [Both notes] “Wild bootstrap standard errors generated using 5,000 replicates, multiplying residuals by draws from the standard normal distribution.”
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: The tests are those of the school-level main effect $\tau$ of SI Eq. (5) and of the interaction coefficient $\beta$ of SI Eq. (6) (standing assumption (S3); P037-T14), for the disciplinary outcome in the 49 schools of the conflict analysis. Tables S6 and S7 with their notes are transcribed in full in P037-T16, and the last sentence of the 2018 Correction, which calls the overall effect statistically insignificant at the 0.05 level, in P037-T15. The publication does not name the variant of the robust variance estimator, gives no sidedness for the tests, and defines the wild bootstrap only by the sentence of the two notes.
canonical_claim.note: Listed because finding P037-N006 (Major) touches it and the brief asks for the statement as printed. The sentences describe a procedure and report two tests; they are not mathematical statements, and Sol's two falsity flags for them are null. Their formalizable content, in this audit's reading and not in the paper's words, is what the procedure is and the two properties a reader takes it to have: that the wild-bootstrap row is a second estimate of the standard error beside the robust row, and that a test at the nominal 5% level with these standard errors has about that size with 49 schools and some twenty regressors. P037-T18 (b) shows that the first is the same quantity as the robust row, and P037-T18 (d) that the variance behind the second is too small in expectation in the homoskedastic benchmark; the size of the test itself is established only by simulation on the public data (note to P037-T18). Lean cannot decide what the $P$ values are on the authors' files. If nothing can be stated beyond P037-T18, not_applicable is the right status for this target. The brief's priority scale has no level for a printed statement that is not a headline result; 3 is used, as for P037-T14 to T17.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Main Methods, the sentence on the 49 schools with administrative data; the Fig. 1 caption; SI Appendix, the paragraph before the list of disciplinary codes, as printed
canonical_claim.location: main p. 567 (PDF p. 2); Fig. 1 caption, main p. 568 (PDF p. 3); SI Appendix p. 10 (supplement PDF p. 10)
canonical_claim.statement:
[Main p. 567, Methods] “In addition to surveys, we tracked behavior using schools' administrative records on peer conflict-related disciplinary events across the entire year (see SI Appendix for materials and methods used). (Administrative data were available for 49 of the 56 schools, and we restricted our attention to these schools for analyses of conflict-related events.)”
[Main p. 568, Fig. 1 caption] “Fig. 1. Overall school climate results: distribution of disciplinary events throughout school networks, comparing treatment, and control schools. Visualization of the effect of treatment on disciplinary reports of peer conflict among the 49 schools that provided administrative data (26 in control, 23 in treatment).”
[SI p. 10, under ‘Codes for administrative disciplinary action (counts summed for each individual and school)’] “Reporting practices for disciplinary events differed across schools. Schools' reporting practices were determined before they were in contact with the research team and before treatment began, and was unrelated to treatment assignment. Codes below represent those used by schools; when schools coded incidents using more detailed categories, those codes were classified within these broader descriptive codes. Any missing data for a student or for an entire category of disciplinary action was treated in our analyses as zero. Seven of 56 schools did not provide any data, for varied reasons including physical document loss, failure to retain documents, and personnel turnover. Failure to provide data was unrelated to treatment status.”
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: The analyses of conflict-related events are the school-level regressions of SI Eqs. (1)–(6) for the disciplinary outcome (Tables S6 and S7, Figs. 1 and 2D), the social-influence estimates for that outcome (Fig. 3D, Table S5) and the corresponding panels of Figs. S5 and S6. The publication gives no rule for deciding that a school provided data other than the sentences above. The rule of the released code is in P037-T19 and P037-T20.
canonical_claim.note: Listed because finding P037-N007 (Moderate) touches it and the brief asks for the statement as printed. The sentences describe the sample; they are not mathematical statements, and Sol's two falsity flags for them are null: the count of 49 (26 control, 23 treatment) is reproduced by the released code on the public data, and whether the seven schools left out provided no usable records originally is not settled. Their formalizable content, in this audit's reading, is the implication a reader draws from them, that the 49 schools are fixed by the availability of records, independently of the assignment and of the outcome, so that the analysis of those schools keeps the causal reading of a randomized comparison. P037-T20 (a) is that implication under assignment-invariant inclusion, and P037-T19 shows that it fails for the outcome-threshold rule that the released code applies. Lean cannot decide what records the schools provided. If nothing can be stated beyond P037-T19 and P037-T20, not_applicable is the right status for this target. Priority 3, as for P037-T14 to T17.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Main Methods, ‘we restricted our network-based analyses to the subpopulation of 2,451 students who had a positive probability of falling into all four levels of exposure’; SI Appendix pp. 14, 18 and 19, and the note to Table S5, as printed
canonical_claim.location: main p. 568 (PDF p. 3); SI Appendix pp. 14, 18 and 19 (supplement PDF pp. 14, 18, 19); Table S5 note, SI p. 40 (supplement PDF p. 40)
canonical_claim.statement:
[Main p. 568, Methods] “In this particular analysis, we restricted our network-based analyses to the subpopulation of 2,451 students who had a positive probability of falling into all four levels of exposure.”
[SI p. 14] “We then restrict ourselves to the subpopulation of students for which there exists some probability that students could receive all four exposures: $0 < \pi_i(d_k) < 1$ for $k \in \{C, S, NI, I\}$.”
[SI p. 18] “We restrict ourselves to the subpopulation of students (n=2451) for which there exists some probability that students could receive all four exposures: $0 < \pi_i(d_k) < 1$ for $k \in \{C, S, NI, I\}$. When $\pi_i(d_k) = 0$ for some students, then the design-based – i.e., extrapolation-free – estimation of average potential outcomes and causal effects must be restricted to the subset of students for which $\pi_i(d_k) > 0$. We will elaborate on this point shortly.”
[SI p. 19, after the display of $\widehat{\mu_R}(d_k)$] “where $N_s$ denotes the number of students such that $0 < \pi_i(d_k) < 1$ for all $i$ and for $k \in \{C, S, NI, I\}$. Note that if any students were to have $\pi_i(d_k) = 0$ in the population under study, then the estimator would be undefined by virtue of division by zero. This implies that the subpopulation under study is restricted to those students who are connected to at least one seed-eligible non-social referent and at least one seed-eligible social referent. Thus our estimates of social influence effects are limited to this subpopulation, which constitutes 2,451 students.”
[Table S5 note, SI p. 40] “Estimates of average potential outcomes using covariate-adjusted inverse probability weighting estimator detailed in the Supplementary Information section Analysis of Social Influence Effects, computed on the subpopulation of 2,451 students who had a positive probability of falling into all four levels of exposure. Standard errors (in parentheses) are computed under a maintained hypothesis of constant effects. Contrasts represent causal differences in outcomes attributable to different configurations of treated peers. A graphical version of this table is presented in Figure 4 in the main text of the paper.”
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: $\pi_i(d_k)$, the exposures $d_C, d_S, d_{NI}, d_I, d_D$ and the estimator $\widehat{\mu_R}(d_k)$ with its summation set $\{i : \pi_i(d_k) > 0, \forall k \in \{C,S,NI,I\}\}$ and its denominator $N_s$ (SI pp. 17–19; standing assumption (S5); P037-T7, P037-T11, P037-T42). SI p. 17: ‘we will not consider the directly treated seed condition exposure, $d_D$, and instead will consider only $d_C, d_S, d_{NI}$ and $d_I$’. Table S5 has four outcome columns and one population for all of them. The reference to ‘Figure 4’ in the note is to Fig. 3 (finding P037-E010, an editorial slip, not a target).
canonical_claim.note: Listed because finding P037-N025 (Moderate) touches it and the brief asks for the statement as printed. The passages define a population and state its size; as a definition, $\{i : 0 < \pi_i(d_k) < 1\ \forall k\}$ is coherent, and the implication printed on SI p. 19 (a student of that population is connected to an eligible referent and to an eligible non-referent) is a true necessary condition which Sol does not dispute. What the finding establishes is that this is not the set on which the released code computes and averages (P037-T22), and P037-T21 shows that the two rules select different students under the paper's design. The number 2,451 is an empirical count that Lean cannot check; it is not reproduced on the public data and is not shown wrong on the authors' files. If nothing can be stated beyond P037-T21 and P037-T22, not_applicable is the right status for this target. Priority 3, as for P037-T14 to T17.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Fig. 2, caption and panel keys, and Fig. S6, caption and panel keys of the school-level panels, as printed
canonical_claim.location: main p. 569 (PDF p. 4), Fig. 2; SI Appendix p. 33 (supplement PDF p. 33), Fig. S6
canonical_claim.statement:
[Fig. 2, main p. 569; key of each of the panels A–D] “Control schools' predicted mean (and 95% CI)” (red line) and “Treatment schools' predicted mean (and 95% CI)” (black line); horizontal axis “Proportion of social referent seeds in anti-conflict group”.
[Fig. 2 caption] “Fig. 2. (A–D) Average school-level climate differences between treatment and control schools caused by anticonflict groups; differences shown to vary with the proportion of social referent seeds in the group. Lines represent estimates of the conditional average potential outcome with respect to the proportion of social referent seeds, and are surrounded by 95% confidence intervals estimated using heteroskedasticity-robust SEs for the regression fit. In examples (A) talking about conflict with friends, (C) wearing anticonflict wristbands, and (D) disciplinary reports of peer conflict, we find evidence that the intervention caused average overall school differences in talking about conflict, wearing anticonflict wristbands, and in actual peer conflict as reported by the school. We find that a higher proportion of social referent seeds assigned to the anticonflict group increases the size of the overall school effect on disciplinary reports of peer conflict ($P$ = 0.07, heteroskedasticity-robust Wald test). See SI Appendix, Table S7 for regression tables.”
[Fig. S6, SI p. 33] Title: “Fig. S6. Re-analysis of Fig. 2 and 3 using betweenness in place of indegree”. Panels (a)–(d) carry the same two keys; horizontal axis “Proportion of high betweenness seeds in anti-conflict group”. Caption: “Average school-level climate effects caused by anti-conflict groups, interacted with proportion of high betweenness seeds in the group. Lines represent estimates of the conditional average potential outcome with respect to the proportion of high betweenness seeds, and are surrounded by 95% confidence intervals estimated using heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors for the regression fit.”
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: The lines are the predictions of the interaction model, SI Eq. (6) (Eq. (2) with covariates; P037-T14), for control schools and for treatment schools as a function of the seed-group composition; Table S7 is the table of that regression (P037-T16). The panels are titled ‘Friends talked to me about conflict’, ‘Perceived social norm against conflict’, ‘Wearing anti-conflict wristband’ and ‘Peer conflict (disciplinary records)’. In each panel the bands are dashed curves on either side of the two lines. The caption does not say how the 95% intervals were computed beyond ‘heteroskedasticity-robust SEs for the regression fit’.
canonical_claim.note: Listed because finding P037-N026 (Moderate) touches it and the brief asks for the statement as printed. A caption is a description of a display, not a theorem; its formalizable content is the identification it makes: that the band round each line is the 95% interval of that group's predicted mean computed from the heteroskedasticity-robust covariance of the regression that gives the line, that is, $\hat m_g(c) \pm 1.96\sqrt{\ell_g(c)\hat V\ell_g(c)'}$ (P037-T24 (b)). The released code computes two other quantities (P037-T24 (d), (e)), and P037-T23 gives a data set in which both differ from it. Lean cannot decide what was drawn in the published figure; the validators' measurements of the printed panels agree with the code's formulas within 0.002. If nothing can be stated beyond P037-T23 and P037-T24, not_applicable is the right status for this target. The significance statement of the caption is P037-T37. Priority 3, as for P037-T14 to T17.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: SI Appendix, the definition of $\theta_i$, $\gamma$ and the two counts of seed peers in the exposure mapping; main Methods, the network question and the four conditions of exposure, as printed
canonical_claim.location: SI Appendix p. 17 (supplement PDF p. 17); main p. 567 (PDF p. 2) and p. 568 (PDF p. 3)
canonical_claim.statement:
[SI p. 17] “Define $D_i = f(\mathbf{Z},\theta_i)$ such that $\Pr(D_i = d) = \pi_i(d)$. We define the exposure mapping as a function, $f(\mathbf{z},\theta_i)$, such that the parameter, $\theta_i$, equals student $i$'s row in the network adjacency matrix. Further let $\gamma$ be an $N$-length vector denoting referent vs. nonreferent status, so that the $j$th element of $\gamma$ takes on the value 1 if student $j$ has an indegree in the top decile of student $j$'s school, and 0 otherwise. The crossproduct of $z_i$ and $\theta_i$, $\mathbf{z}'\theta_i$, is equal to the number of student $i$'s peers that are assigned to be seeds. Further $(\mathbf{z}\circ\gamma)'\theta_i$ is equal to the number of student $i$'s referent peers that are assigned to be seeds.”
[Main p. 567, Methods] “The social network question, accompanied by a full student roster for the school, asked students to nominate up to 10 students at their school whom they chose to spend time with in the last few weeks, either in school, out of school, or online.” ... “Our network question (i.e., “whom did you choose to spend time with, face to face or online”) directly measures who is observing whose behavior.”
[Main p. 568, Methods] “We considered four conditions of exposure to the seed students in each school: (i) students in control schools, (ii) students in treated schools for whom no peers are seeds, (iii) students in treated schools for whom at least one peer is a seed but no seed is a social referent, and (iv) students in treated schools for whom at least one peer is a social referent seed.”
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: The exposure mapping that uses these quantities is the display of SI p. 17 (transcribed in P037-T7; corrected in P037-T8); $\mathbf{z}$ is the assignment vector and $\mathbf{Z}$ the random assignment (standing assumption (S5)). The publication does not define ‘the network adjacency matrix’ or ‘peer’ further: the nominations are directed (a student names up to ten others), referents are defined by indegree, and nothing is said about a matrix derived from the nominations. The slip ‘crossproduct of $z_i$ and $\theta_i$’ for the vector $\mathbf{z}$ is part of finding P037-E002 (P037-T8, note).
canonical_claim.note: Listed because finding P037-N032 (Moderate) touches it and the brief asks for the statement as printed. Sol's flags: false as printed, no; false under the natural reading, yes. The passage is a definition, and its two sentences about the counts are true identities for whichever binary matrix is taken as ‘the network adjacency matrix’ (P037-T26 (b) for the either-direction matrix; the same expansion for the matrix of nominations). What is formalizable is therefore not a false statement but an indeterminacy: the definition has two readings, the row of the nominations (the natural reading, with main p. 567) and the row of the either-direction matrix (the one the released code uses), and P037-T25 shows that they give different exposures, probabilities and weights. Lean cannot decide which reading a reader takes. If nothing can be stated beyond P037-T25 and P037-T26, not_applicable is the right status for this target. Priority 3, as for P037-T14 to T17.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: SI Appendix, the covariate-adjusted inverse probability weighted regression estimator $\hat\xi(d_k)$, $\widehat{\mu_R}(d_k)$, and the sentence of main Methods that describes it, as printed
canonical_claim.location: SI Appendix pp. 18–19 (supplement PDF pp. 18–19); main p. 568 (PDF p. 3)
canonical_claim.statement:
[SI pp. 18–19] “We will use a covariate-adjusted inverse probability weighted regression estimator to estimate our average potential outcomes and therefore average causal effects. For covariate adjustment, define an estimated parameter vector associated with exposure condition $d_k$
$$\widehat\xi(d_k) = \arg\min_{\xi(d_k)}\sum_{i : D_i = d_k}\frac{1}{\pi_i(d_k)}\left[y_i(d_k) - g(\mathbf{x_i},\xi(d_k))\right]^2,$$
where $g(.)$ is the specification for the regression of $y_i(d_k)$ on $\mathbf{x_i}$. $\xi(d_k)$ is the parameter vector arising from an inverse probability weighted regression of outcomes on covariates among students in a given level of exposure. Then the regression estimator for the mean is
$$\widehat{\mu_R}(d_k) = \frac{1}{N_s}\sum_{i : \pi_i(d_k) > 0,\ \forall k \in \{C,S,NI,I\}}\left[\mathbf{I}(D_i = d_k)\,\frac{y_i(d_k) - g\big(\mathbf{x_i},\widehat\xi(d_k)\big)}{\hat\pi_i(d_k)} + g\big(\mathbf{x_i},\widehat\xi(d_k)\big)\right],$$
where $N_s$ denotes the number of students such that $0 < \pi_i(d_k) < 1$ for all $i$ and for $k \in \{C, S, NI, I\}$.” ... “Estimation of average causal effects follows using a plug-in estimate, $\hat\mu_R(d_k) - \hat\mu_R(d_l)$.”
[Main p. 568, Methods] “Using inverse probability weighting, a well-known nonparametric correction (48, 49), we used these probabilities to predict population means of potential outcomes (50) for students under different levels of exposure. In practice, this implies weighting each observation by the inverse of its probability of falling into its observed exposure condition in a weighted least-squares regression, and using fitted values from the regression to compute the average predicted value in the population.”
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: $D_i = f(\mathbf{Z},\theta_i)$ is the exposure of student $i$, $\pi_i(d_k)$ its probability and $\hat\pi_i(d_k)$ its simulated estimate (SI pp. 17–18; P037-T9); $y_i(d_k)$ are the fixed potential outcomes and $\mu(d_k)$ their average (standing assumption (S5)). The publication does not specify $g(.)$ further and does not list the covariates $\mathbf{x_i}$ of this regression. In the first display the weight is printed with $\pi_i(d_k)$ and in the second with $\hat\pi_i(d_k)$. Table S5 and Fig. 3 are described as computed with this estimator (Table S5 note, transcribed in P037-T39). The same displays are transcribed in the definitions of P037-T11.
canonical_claim.note: Listed because finding P037-N033 (Moderate) touches it and the brief asks for the statement as printed. The two displays define an estimator and are coherent as a definition (with a linear $g$: P037-T28 (b)); the sentence of the main text is broad enough to cover the released code as well. What the finding establishes is that the reported numbers were computed with a different estimator, one regression with exposure intercepts and common slopes (P037-T28 (a)), on a different averaging set (P037-T22), and P037-T27 shows that the two estimators are not the same function of the data. So the passage has no false mathematical statement to formalize; its formalizable content is the definition itself. If nothing can be stated beyond P037-T27 and P037-T28, not_applicable is the right status for this target. The consistency and asymptotic normality claimed for this estimator on the same page are P037-E004 (P037-T10, T11). Priority 3, as for P037-T14 to T17.
